step_text: The forest was silent that evening, until a figure stepped through the line of cedars and—
—shattered the stillness like a dropped porcelain vase in a cathedral of glass.
The figure was not a man, nor a beast, but a collection of shadows held together by a coat of moth-eaten velvet.
He moved with the heavy, rhythmic gait of a pendulum swinging in a vacuum, each step a bruise upon the moss.
To look at him was to stare into a well of ink during a lunar eclipse; to hear him was to listen to the grinding of tectonic plates beneath a layer of silk.

*I remember when the trees used to speak in a dialect of amber and sap,* the narrator’s voice suddenly shifts, dropping from the detached observation of a chronicler to the trembling intimacy of a survivor.
*But he wasn't part of the forest.
He was a puncture wound in the fabric of the evening, a jagged tear in a tapestry of twilight.
He carried a lantern that didn't glow with fire, but with the pale, sickly luminescence of a dying thought.*

It is worth noting, for the sake of the record, that such apparitions were common during the Era of the Gilded Rust (circa 412 Post-Sunder). During those years, the sky turned the color of a bruised plum, and the Great Clock of Orizon famously began to run backward, causing the citizens of the Lowlands to age in reverse until they were nothing more than weeping infants in silk cradles.

It was a time of profound chronological instability, where a man might breakfast with his grandfather and dine with his unborn grandson, all while the rain fell upward like silver needles seeking the clouds.
The figure stopped.
He reached into his velvet coat and pulled out a compass that spun with the frantic energy of a trapped hummingbird.
The needle didn't point North; it pointed toward *regret*.
*He looked at me,* the voice whispers, now a frantic, staccato rhythm, *and his eyes were two abandoned shipwrecks resting on a seabed of starlight.
I felt my courage evaporating like dew on a hot griddle, leaving me as hollow as a dried gourd in a desert of salt.
I wanted to run, but my legs were pillars of salt, and my heart was a frantic bird beating against the cage of my ribs.*
The figure spoke, but the sound was not a voice.
It was the sound of a thousand pages turning in a library at the bottom of the ocean.
"The debt is overdue," the sound vibrated through the marrow of the trees.
"The interest has grown like ivy on a tombstone, choking the very memory of the principal."
Suddenly, the ground beneath the cedars began to ripple.
The earth was no longer solid; it had become a sea of liquid obsidian, undulating with the slow, hypnotic grace of a sleeping leviathan.
The trees did not fall; they drifted, their roots unspooling like the frayed ends of a cosmic sweater.
*Wait,* a new voice interjects—a cold, clinical, third-person perspective, reminiscent of a surgeon documenting a terminal case.
*The subject's perception of reality is fracturing.
The spatial dimensions are behaving like a spilled inkwell on a linen sheet, blurring the boundaries between the observer and the observed.
The forest is not disappearing; it is being rewritten by a hand that finds the current syntax of existence to be insufficiently poetic.*
As the landscape dissolved, a structure began to rise from the obsidian waves.
It was a tower of bone and clockwork, spiraling upward like a scream frozen in mid-air.
This was the Spire of Malakor, a relic from the Age of the Unspoken Vow, when the architects of the Old World discovered that stone could be taught to dream if it was fed enough secrets.

It is a historical fact that the Spire was built using the calcified sighs of poets, which explains why the walls vibrate with a melancholy that can induce spontaneous weeping in even the most stoic of travelers.
The figure in the velvet coat began to climb.
He did not use stairs; he walked upon the air as if it were a staircase of solidified moonlight.
*I followed him,* the survivor's voice cries out, a desperate, jagged thing.
*I was a moth drawn to a funeral pyre, a leaf caught in a gale of destiny.
I climbed because the alternative was to drown in the silence of the cedars, which had become as heavy as a mountain of lead.*
As they ascended, the stars above began to rearrange themselves.
They were no longer distant suns, but glowing embers tossed into a hearth of infinite blackness.
The constellations shifted, forming the shape of a giant, unblinking eye that watched their progress with the indifference of a god watching an ant struggle with a crumb.
*The air grew thin, tasting of copper and old memories,* the narrator observes, the voice now settling into a weary, rhythmic drone.
*The climb was a slow descent into the belly of a dream, a journey through a corridor of mirrors where every reflection was a lie told by a beautiful stranger.
We were moving through time as if it were thick honey, each second a heavy, golden weight that threatened to crush the very concept of 'now'.*
Halfway up the Spire, the figure stopped again.
He turned, and for the first time, the velvet coat fell open.
There was no body inside.
There was only a miniature galaxy, swirling in a vortex of violet and gold, a tiny, contained universe spinning within the hollow shell of a man.
"You are late," the galaxy whispered, the sound echoing like a bell struck underwater.
"The stars have already begun to forget your name."<turn|>_
